posts.name: Gregory Brew
posts.text:
For Iran, today's summit was a strategic victory, even if it generates no successful effort at a favorable deal with the US ahead of what appears to be very likely escalation.

A few reasons why:

-Iran has strived for years to create a regional order that isolates Israel and excludes the US. Today's meeting is a move in that direction, though a very small one.

-The context for the summit is not the Mecca partner's desire to include Iran, or grow closer to it, but their collective alarm at Iran's willingness to attack them, as well as other states, in response to US attacks. For Iran, this engagement justifies the strategy--regional states must engage Iran, and on Iran's terms, for the sake of their own security. (This feeds into the issue above--the US, it is presumed, can no longer satisfy this security requirement). 

-the Mecca partners came to Tehran--almost as if they were summoned. Why Iranian media made such a big show of this: coming at a time when Israeli and US officials seem once again tempted by regime change through military force, an event like this can be spun as a way to affirm the Islamic Republic's international legitimacy. 

-subtext for the visit is the Mecca partner's acknowledgement that the Islamic Republic isn't going anywhere--not matter how intense US pressure becomes, or how violent the next round of escalation may be. For the regime, survival has been the first priority this year. An event like this confirms the regime's sense that the region--no matter how much its inhabitants alternatively hate and fear Iran--has no alternative but to accept its existence as a fact of life. 

To be clear, this is how the regime is likely to view these events, and why Rezaee and others are spending so much time emphasizing the day's diplomatic engagement, even if they are unlikely to prove especially fruitful.

posts.text:
I went the other way and asked @grok what companies that currently don't exist that might be major players in the future:

Here’s a speculative list of companies that largely don’t exist (or are only embryonic) today but could be major players by ~2031–2036, based on current trajectories in AI, biotech, energy, space, robotics, and climate tech.

These are extrapolations from things already showing real momentum (WEF’s 2026 emerging tech list, McKinsey’s future arenas, progress in humanoids, precision fermentation, BCIs, lithium extraction, etc.), not pure sci-fi. Timelines and winners are highly uncertain—many will fail or get absorbed.

Speculative future companies:

AetherGrid (or similar V2G/everything-to-grid platforms)
Aggregates millions of EVs, home batteries, and idle storage into virtual power plants that stabilize grids in real time. Turns “sitting” energy assets into a paid service as renewables grow and peak demand becomes a bigger problem.

HelixForge / PerfectProtein
Large-scale precision fermentation factories producing animal-identical proteins, dairy, eggs, and specialized ingredients cheaper and more consistently than livestock or traditional agriculture. Moves from niche supplements to mainstream food supply chains.

SynapseLink (commercial BCI)
Consumer/enterprise brain-computer interfaces (building on Neuralink-style work) for communication, cognitive tools, rehabilitation, or high-bandwidth human-AI interaction. Early medical use expands into productivity and accessibility markets.

VitaSpan Clinics (longevity networks)
Personalized gene therapy, senolytic, and AI-guided anti-aging clinics that deliver measurable healthspan extension. Gene editing, mRNA platforms, and biomarkers mature enough for routine (if expensive) clinical use beyond rare diseases.

OrbitalHarvest / LunarExtract
Resource extraction from the Moon or near-Earth asteroids delivering water, metals, or propellant for in-space use (and eventually Earth). Launch costs keep falling and early missions prove economics for cislunar logistics.

CarbonVault / PFASBreak
Industrial-scale direct air capture + permanent sequestration, or specialized destruction of “forever chemicals.” Becomes a regulated infrastructure business as carbon accounting and chemical cleanup mandates tighten.

RoboNexus / HouseholdFleet
Operators of fleets of general-purpose humanoid robots for elder care, cleaning, logistics, and light industrial work on a subscription or service model. Hardware costs drop and reliability crosses the “useful every day” threshold.

BioPrint Organics
Bioprinted tissues and organs for transplant. Moves from experimental to regulated clinical products that meaningfully reduce waiting lists for certain organs.

SkyLink Air (urban air mobility operator)
eVTOL networks providing short-haul city-to-city or intra-urban flights as an alternative to ground traffic. Certification, battery, and infrastructure progress turns prototypes into scheduled services in major metros.

AgentOS / PersonalAgent Co.
The dominant “life OS” layer of highly capable personal AI agents that manage calendars, finances, health data, shopping, and work across services. Agents become the primary interface rather than apps.

QuantumShield / QaaS platforms
Quantum-resistant cryptography and practical quantum computing services (optimization, simulation, materials) sold to enterprises and governments as classical crypto faces real threats and quantum advantage appears in niche domains.

OrbitalForge
In-space manufacturing of advanced materials, semiconductors, or fiber optics that benefit from microgravity. Early commercial production runs for high-value products.

Honorable mentions / longer-shot but plausible:

A first commercial fusion power operator (still ambitious for 5–10 years but accelerating).

Large-scale biomining or engineered-microbe critical mineral recovery companies.

Fully modular, AI-designed, robotic-constructed housing firms focused on climate-resilient

Here's a basic answer to this frequently asked question, courtesy of Rob Kaplan, who used to have the same job: "So let's talk about what a supply shock is, and I'll give you my own two cents on it. If you have a supply shock and it lasts for two months, then I think the knee-jerk reaction if you're at the Fed is, "Let's just wait and do nothing, and we'll look through it."

"If you have a supply shock, on the other hand, that goes on for six, seven, eight months and maybe it could go on for a lot longer, what happens is it begins to bleed into 30 or 40 items, and then a year or two later you forget how the inflation even started. So that's why those who say supply shock, what can a Fed funds rate increase do about it?"

"Well, one thing it can do is prevent the bleed or slow the bleed to 30 or 40 other items. And Warsh even commented on that, and he was right to do it in the press conference. We can't stop the oil shock, but we can slow down maybe the transmission to other items. And I do think they've realized at this point they need to be focused on doing that."

posts.name: Anthony Pompliano 🌪
posts.text:
I spent years thinking I’d never get married or have kids. Now I come home to my best friend and 4 kids yelling ‘Dad!!’ as they run at me. To me, that is success. Here’s why:

Success was always something I had difficulty defining. One individual may measure success by money in the bank. Another may place importance on their professional accolades. And someone else may define it via their material possessions. Each person is optimizing for something different.

Eventually, I found a description of success that resonated and became my personal definition.

WHOOP founder @willahmed  said, “Success is being excited to go to work and being excited to come home.”

What a perfect encapsulation of how I view the world. 

In my perspective, success has never been about a number, an award, or any single accomplishment. Frankly, I like to compete too much to ever admit I have ‘made it,’ so my definition of success is naturally more about the process of my life rather than a specific outcome.

A large percentage of people do not enjoy their job. They either dislike their industry, company, or colleagues. They may stay in the situation because the money is attractive or they are scared to leave for the unknown. Regardless of the reason, these individuals are unhappy for a large chunk of their day.

Many people are also dissatisfied with their personal lives. Some are single and frustrated that they haven’t found the right partner, while others are married but unhappy because they feel like strangers in their own home. And plenty of people have health or financial issues that are gnawing at them daily.

Although I have faced similar daily struggles as others, I have always felt fortunate that I enjoyed going to work and coming home each day. 

Professionally, I sacrificed my time and short-term potential earnings in order to work on what truly mattered to me. I was able to become my own boss and design a career that was satisfying and exciting.

The excitement in my personal life is entirely because of my wife and my kids. Getting married and having children has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my life. There is nothing better than walking in the door after a long day of work and hearing the sound of little kids yell “Dad!!” as they run towards me to give me a hug. 

@polinapompliano and I are genuinely each other’s best friend. We enjoy spending the majority of our time together and we feed off each other’s energy and ambition. Maybe most importantly, we are happiest when we talk about ideas and help make each other’s dreams come true.

I am just as excited to go to work as I am to come home. I know it is probably rare, but I have achieved all the success I ever wanted.

My hope for you is that you can do the same.

This is an excerpt from my new book, How To Live An Extraordinary Life Volume 2. You can buy a copy of the book here: https://www.amazon.com/How-Live-Extraordinary-Life-Two/dp/1804094153/

quoted.text:
Krishna Rao is the CFO of Anthropic, and this is his first podcast appearance.

He joined the company two years ago when run-rate revenue was about $250M. Today it is $30B. He has helped raise ~$75B and is responsible for the procurement and allocation of compute.

I feel lucky we get to hear what it is like to sit inside a company this consequential at a moment this pivotal.

We discuss:
- The cone of uncertainty
- How he allocates compute across Trainium, TPUs, and GPUs
- What investors misunderstand about model companies
- Why the returns to frontier intelligence keep rising

posts.text:
🇺🇸 War, AI and politics have more people second guessing whether to start a family... and fear may be the worst reason to wait.

Keith McCullough tells people not to let fear make that call for them, and he doesn’t pretend the risks are small:

“The truth is dangerous.”

He sees every cycle of concentrated power eventually breaking, with the next generation left to build whatever comes after.

That turns having kids now into a bet on the rebuild, and the bet only pays off if people actually make it.

@KeithMcCullough

quoted.text:
🇺🇸 AI has been carrying the US economy... and if the bubble breaks, growth could sink to 1% within nine months.

The AI boom helped power jobs, wealth and a third quarter the Atlanta Fed tracks at 3.5% growth. Keith McCullough’s model has that sliding to 2%, then 1%, over the next six to nine months.

He also argues this market is running on far more leverage than in 1999, the last time a tech bubble burst.

If AI was the gas pedal for growth, a crash would hit jobs and paychecks right along with portfolios.

@KeithMcCullough
